newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canada doubts but aid agencies seek Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: Canada doubts but aid agencies seek Zaire mission.

text.p: With some countries wavering over plans to send a peace force to Zaire, aid agencies insist the crisis is far from over and would welcome an armed force to help them in their relief work.

Canada, tapped to lead the U.N.'s newest emergency force, joined the think-again brigade on Monday as the world struggled to assess how hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees streaming home from Zaire altered a crisis which last week had seemed to threaten well over a million people.
Defence Minister Doug Young told reporters in Ottawa that, if conditions in the heart of Africa continued to improve, the force could be scaled back to humanitarian relief units.

"If we get the results hoped for, and people can return to their home countries, and humanitarian organisations can do their work without being in danger, then the mission becomes unnecessary," Young said.
"No one wants to go to Zaire or Rwanda for Christmas."

The United States has put its commitment to the force on hold and some countries have been lukewarm from the start about the force, which was intended to get food to refugees in eastern Zaire and perhaps clear a route for them to go home.
But France and Spain, the first and strongest advocates of intervention, said on Monday they still wanted to go.
"For the moment I think it's still necessary," Xavier Emmanuelli, French secretary of state for emergency humanitarian action, told a French television channel from the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
Spain's Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told Reuters television the mass return to Rwanda was partly the result of word that an international force would soon be on it way.
"The operation needs retouching, but in our opinion it should be maintained," he said.

Aid agencies estimate there are still some 700,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, scattered by a three-cornered conflict among Zairean Tutsis rebels, refugee Hutu extremists and the Zairean army.
According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, hundreds of thousands of Zaireans uprooted by the fighting also need help.

Red Cross spokeswoman Nina Winquist told Reuters an ICRC medical team pushed 35 kms (17 miles) south of Goma on Monday and discovered a hospital at Kirotshe which was crammed to capacity with 75 patients, including 60 war wounded.
Ray Wilkinson, spokeman for the U.N.'s refugee agency, said UNHCR was still focussing on the mass exodus and its implications for Rwanda.
"This is a new beginning for Rwanda," he said. "For the past two years Rwanda has been a country waiting for its soul to return -- now it can start rebuilding."
However, some aid workers, who asked for anonymity, said the UNHCR was colluding with the Rwandan government in seeking to speed all the refugees, some exhausted and sick, to their home villages.

The Rwandan government on Monday started to clear refugees camps away from the border with Zaire, forcing 350 sick people out of a camp run by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies inside Unbano camp, four kms (two miles) from the border.
The 350 were taken away in trucks. No violence was used, but the Red Cross is to protest to the Rwandan government.

The flow of refugees out of Zaire into Rwanda slowed on Monday but could pick up again if Zaire's Tutsi rebels, who have close links with Kigali, open a corridor in the Bukavu region so tens of thousands of refugees further south can also go home.

UNHCR spokesman Fernando Del Mundo said in Geneva the rebels told U.N. agencies that the corridor from Bukavu, south of Lake Kivu, to Rwanda's southwestern Cyangugu border crossing could be opened on Tuesday.
If those refugees start to reach home, in addition to the 500,000 already estimated by UNHCR to have returned, the argument in favour of the peace force will be weakened again.

Perhaps reflecting the lack of urgency now felt by the countries that had agreed to help, a review meeting planned for Wednesday in Stuttgart, Germany, was put back to Thursday. No explanation was given.
The United Nations Department of Humanitarian Affairs issued an urgent appeal on Monday for $260 million to fund relief for refugees in eastern Zaire.
